Reference: Baqaee and Farhi (2019)

Model Setting

The paper asks how a productivity shock to one producer affects aggregate output once the analysis goes beyond the first order. Hulten's theorem (Hulten 1978) states that in an efficient economy the first-order effect of a microeconomic productivity shock on aggregate output equals the producer's sales as a share of GDP, its Domar weight. The theorem implies that the production network, the elasticities of substitution, returns to scale and the scope for factor reallocation are irrelevant given observed sales, which is why Gabaix (2016) could describe networks as a particular case of granularity. The paper argues that this conclusion rests on a fragile first-order approximation. Walmart and electricity production each have sales of roughly 4 percent of US GDP, yet a large negative shock to electricity should be far more damaging. The paper derives a general second-order approximation of aggregate output for any efficient economy. Because the first derivative of log output is the Domar weight, the second derivative is the response of the Domar weight to the shock. This response is first expressed with reduced-form sufficient statistics (general equilibrium elasticities of substitution and the elasticity of the input-output multiplier) and then mapped to microeconomic primitives for nested-CES economies with arbitrary input-output linkages, and for arbitrary production functions.

The main findings are as follows. Cobb-Douglas economies are a knife-edge case in which Domar weights and the whole input-output matrix are constant, the model is log-linear and Hulten's approximation is globally exact. Away from this case the second-order terms depend on microeconomic elasticities of substitution, network linkages, returns to scale and the degree of factor reallocation. With complementarities, nonlinearities amplify negative shocks and attenuate positive shocks, so that symmetric and thin-tailed sectoral shocks produce an output distribution with a lower mean, negative skewness and excess kurtosis. In a calibrated multi-sector model the mean output loss from sectoral shocks is between 0.2 and 1.3 percent, an order of magnitude above the welfare cost of business cycles of Lucas (1987). Nonlinearities almost triple the estimated effect of the 1970s oil shocks on world output, from 0.23 to 0.61 percent, and account for a reduction of about 20 percentage points in US aggregate TFP growth over 1948-2014 (Baumol's cost disease).

Two reduced-form objects describe how Domar weights move. For any smooth function fff of (A1,…,AN)(A_1,\dots,A_N)(A1​,…,AN​) with partial derivatives fif_ifi​, the pseudo elasticity of substitution ρji\rho_{ji}ρji​ is defined by the first equality below; applied to the aggregate output function it is the GE elasticity of substitution, and Hulten's theorem then gives the second equality:

When fff is homogeneous of degree one, ρji\rho_{ji}ρji​ coincides with the Morishima elasticity of substitution. Good jjj is a GE-complement for iii if ρji∈(0,1)\rho_{ji}\in(0,1)ρji​∈(0,1), in which case a fall in the productivity of iii raises λi/λj\lambda_i/\lambda_jλi​/λj​, and a GE-substitute otherwise. These elasticities are equilibrium objects that embed reallocation and network effects, and the relation is not symmetric in general. The input-output multiplier is:

ξ≡∑i=1Ndlog⁡Ydlog⁡Ai=∑i=1Nλi(4.11.8.5)\xi\equiv\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{d\log Y}{d\log A_i}=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i \tag{4.11.8.5}ξ≡i=1∑N​dlogAi​dlogY​=i=1∑N​λi​(4.11.8.5)

It is the percentage response of output to a uniform one percent increase in technology. It exceeds one when there are intermediate inputs, because goods are reproducible, and it can be read as a measure of aggregate returns to scale. Its response dlog⁡ξ/dlog⁡Aid\log\xi/d\log A_idlogξ/dlogAi​ measures substitution between the underlying factors (whose payments are GDP) and reproducible goods (whose payments are sales).

The first term is the Lucas cost from curvature in utility, which is small in practice. The second term comes from curvature in production, does not depend on γ\gammaγ, and is present even with linear utility. The two sources of loss do not interact up to the second order. With GE-substitutability the production term is positive, and a risk-averse household may prefer a stochastic economy.

The parameter ωg\omega_gωg​ indexes reallocation: ωg=0\omega_g=0ωg​=0 means that labor cannot be reallocated (equivalently, extreme decreasing returns), and ωg=1\omega_g=1ωg​=1 means full reallocation with constant returns.

The proof solves for the allocation of general labor and substitutes it into the consumption aggregator, which yields a CES function of the AiA_iAi​ with elasticity ρ\rhoρ. With no reallocation ρ=θ0\rho=\theta_0ρ=θ0​ and the second-order term is λi(1−λi)(1−1/θ0)\lambda_i(1-\lambda_i)(1-1/\theta_0)λi​(1−λi​)(1−1/θ0​). Relative quantities yi/yjy_i/y_jyi​/yj​ move one for one with the shock, and relative prices pi/pjp_i/p_jpi​/pj​ move more than one for one when θ0<1\theta_0<1θ0​<1, so the relative share of a producer hit by a negative shock rises. In the Leontief limit θ0→0\theta_0\to0θ0​→0 the relative price and share jump to infinity after a negative shock and to zero after a positive shock, and the first-order term is uninformative. With full reallocation ρ=1/(2−θ0)\rho=1/(2-\theta_0)ρ=1/(2−θ0​) and the second-order term is λi(1−λi)(θ0−1)\lambda_i(1-\lambda_i)(\theta_0-1)λi​(1−λi​)(θ0​−1). Relative prices now move inversely one for one with the shock, and labor flows toward the shocked producer after a negative shock when θ0<1\theta_0<1θ0​<1, which reinforces the weak link. A near-Leontief technology is therefore not sufficient for large deviations from Hulten's theorem when factors can be reallocated. The singular case moves to the perfect-substitutes limit, where all labor goes to the most productive producer. In both cases the second-order term is zero at θ0=1\theta_0=1θ0​=1, negative for θ0<1\theta_0<1θ0​<1 and positive for θ0>1\theta_0>1θ0​>1, and it scales with λi(1−λi)\lambda_i(1-\lambda_i)λi​(1−λi​), so it is largest for producers of intermediate size. In short, complementarities with immobile labor make negative shocks very costly, and substitutabilities with mobile labor make positive shocks very beneficial.

Hulten's approximation is exact only without intermediate inputs (ξ=1\xi=1ξ=1) or with Cobb-Douglas technology (θ1=1\theta_1=1θ1​=1). Because output is its own input, when θ1<1\theta_1<1θ1​<1 a negative shock raises the expenditure share on the intermediate input and hence the multiplier, and a positive shock lowers it; the effect grows with the network term ξ(ξ−1)\xi(\xi-1)ξ(ξ−1). Gross output is homogeneous in productivity, but aggregate value added is not homogeneous of any degree. In the limit θ1→0\theta_1\to0θ1​→0 output is linear, and not log-linear, in productivity with slope 1/ω1l1/\omega_{1l}1/ω1l​.

Nested-CES Economies in Standard Form

Any nested-CES economy with a representative consumer can be relabeled so that every CES aggregator is a node of the network with a single elasticity of substitution. This standard form has N+1+FN+1+FN+1+F nodes: node 000 is the household, nodes 111 to NNN are reproducible goods, and the last FFF nodes are factors, which are endowments with yf/y‾f=1y_f/\overline{y}_f=1yf​/y​f​=1. The reproducible nodes 0≤i≤N0\leq i\leq N0≤i≤N have production functions:

with ∑j=1N+Fωij=1\sum_{j=1}^{N+F}\omega_{ij}=1∑j=1N+F​ωij​=1, Y/Y‾=y0/y‾0Y/\overline{Y}=y_0/\overline{y}_0Y/Y=y0​/y​0​ and market clearing yi=∑j=0Nxjiy_i=\sum_{j=0}^Nx_{ji}yi​=∑j=0N​xji​. The steady-state input-output matrix, the Leontief inverse and the input-output covariance operator are:

The operator is the covariance between the iiith and jjjth columns of the Leontief inverse, Ψ(i)\Psi_{(i)}Ψ(i)​ and Ψ(j)\Psi_{(j)}Ψ(j)​, using the kkkth row of Ω\OmegaΩ (the expenditure shares of producer kkk) as the probability distribution; VarΩ(k)(Ψ(i))Var_{\Omega^{(k)}}(\Psi_{(i)})VarΩ(k)​(Ψ(i)​) denotes the case i=ji=ji=j.

One Factor

A single factor means that primary factors are perfectly substitutable and fully reallocated.

Proposition 7 (second-order network centrality). In a nested-CES model in standard form with a single factor:

d2log⁡Ydlog⁡Aj dlog⁡Ai=dλidlog⁡Aj=∑k=0N(θk−1)λkCovΩ(k)(Ψ(i),Ψ(j))d2log⁡Ydlog⁡Ai2=dλidlog⁡Ai=∑k=0N(θk−1)λkVarΩ(k)(Ψ(i))(4.11.8.18)\begin{aligned} \frac{d^2\log Y}{d\log A_j\,d\log A_i}&=\frac{d\lambda_i}{d\log A_j}=\sum_{k=0}^N(\theta_k-1)\lambda_kCov_{\Omega^{(k)}}\left(\Psi_{(i)},\Psi_{(j)}\right)\\ \frac{d^2\log Y}{d\log A_i^2}&=\frac{d\lambda_i}{d\log A_i}=\sum_{k=0}^N(\theta_k-1)\lambda_kVar_{\Omega^{(k)}}\left(\Psi_{(i)}\right) \end{aligned} \tag{4.11.8.18}dlogAj​dlogAi​d2logY​dlogAi2​d2logY​​=dlogAj​dλi​​=k=0∑N​(θk​−1)λk​CovΩ(k)​(Ψ(i)​,Ψ(j)​)=dlogAi​dλi​​=k=0∑N​(θk​−1)λk​VarΩ(k)​(Ψ(i)​)​(4.11.8.18)

The intuition is as follows. After a negative shock to jjj, the vector of price changes is proportional to the exposures Ψ(j)\Psi_{(j)}Ψ(j)​. A producer kkk with θk<1\theta_k<1θk​<1 raises its expenditure share on the inputs whose prices rise more. This raises demand for iii if those inputs are also more exposed to iii, as measured by Ψ(i)\Psi_{(i)}Ψ(i)​. The effect is larger when the covariance is larger, when kkk is larger (λk\lambda_kλk​), and when θk\theta_kθk​ is further from one. Substitution by kkk is irrelevant if kkk is small or is exposed to iii equally through all of its inputs. The diagonal expression is a centrality measure that combines elasticities with network structure. The GE elasticities and the multiplier elasticity are recovered from the same derivatives:

1−1ρji=dlog⁡λidlog⁡Ai−dlog⁡λjdlog⁡Ai,dlog⁡ξdlog⁡Ai=1ξ∑jλjdlog⁡λjdlog⁡Ai(4.11.8.19)1-\frac{1}{\rho_{ji}}=\frac{d\log\lambda_i}{d\log A_i}-\frac{d\log\lambda_j}{d\log A_i},\qquad\frac{d\log\xi}{d\log A_i}=\frac{1}{\xi}\sum_j\lambda_j\frac{d\log\lambda_j}{d\log A_i} \tag{4.11.8.19}1−ρji​1​=dlogAi​dlogλi​​−dlogAi​dlogλj​​,dlogAi​dlogξ​=ξ1​j∑​λj​dlogAi​dlogλj​​(4.11.8.19)

Corollary 1 (network irrelevance). Suppose there is a single factor, θj=θ\theta_j=\thetaθj​=θ for every jjj, and shocks are factor-augmenting, that is, they hit only producers whose sole input is the primary factor. Then output has a closed form and:

YY‾=(∑i=0Nλ‾iAiθ−1)1θ−1,dλidlog⁡Aj=(θ−1)λi(1(i=j)−λj)(4.11.8.20)\frac{Y}{\overline{Y}}=\left(\sum_{i=0}^N\overline{\lambda}_iA_i^{\theta-1}\right)^{\frac{1}{\theta-1}},\qquad\frac{d\lambda_i}{d\log A_j}=(\theta-1)\lambda_i\left(\mathbf{1}(i=j)-\lambda_j\right) \tag{4.11.8.20}YY​=(i=0∑N​λi​Aiθ−1​)θ−11​,dlogAj​dλi​​=(θ−1)λi​(1(i=j)−λj​)(4.11.8.20)

where λ‾i\overline{\lambda}_iλi​ is the steady-state Domar weight. The diagonal term is (θ−1)λi(1−λi)(\theta-1)\lambda_i(1-\lambda_i)(θ−1)λi​(1−λi​). Factor-augmenting shocks hold ξ\xiξ constant at one, and uniform elasticities make the GE elasticities uniform at ρji=1/(2−θ)\rho_{ji}=1/(2-\theta)ρji​=1/(2−θ). Domar weights and θ\thetaθ are then sufficient statistics, locally and globally, even though Hulten's approximation fails. Relaxing either condition makes the network matter.

Energy example. Energy is produced linearly from labor with productivity AeA_eAe​. Each of NNN downstream producers combines labor and energy with elasticity θ1\theta_1θ1​ and sells to the household, which substitutes across final goods with elasticity θ0\theta_0θ0​, where θ1<1\theta_1<1θ1​<1 and θ1<θ0\theta_1<\theta_0θ1​<θ0​. All final sectors have λi=1/N\lambda_i=1/Nλi​=1/N; M≤NM\leq NM≤N of them use energy with the same input share ωe\omega_eωe​, the others use none, and ωe\omega_eωe​ is chosen so that the sales share of energy λe\lambda_eλe​ stays constant as MMM varies. Proposition 7 gives:

d2log⁡Ydlog⁡Ae2=λe2(NM−1)(θ0−1)+λe(1−NMλe)(θ1−1)=λe(1−λe)(θ0−1)+λe(1−NMλe)(θ1−θ0)(4.11.8.21)\begin{aligned} \frac{d^2\log Y}{d\log A_e^2}&=\lambda_e^2\left(\frac{N}{M}-1\right)(\theta_0-1)+\lambda_e\left(1-\frac{N}{M}\lambda_e\right)(\theta_1-1)\\ &=\lambda_e(1-\lambda_e)(\theta_0-1)+\lambda_e\left(1-\frac{N}{M}\lambda_e\right)(\theta_1-\theta_0) \end{aligned} \tag{4.11.8.21}dlogAe2​d2logY​​=λe2​(MN​−1)(θ0​−1)+λe​(1−MN​λe​)(θ1​−1)=λe​(1−λe​)(θ0​−1)+λe​(1−MN​λe​)(θ1​−θ0​)​(4.11.8.21)

The first line weights each elasticity by the dispersion of exposure to energy across the inputs of the corresponding node, with VarΩ(0)(Ψ(e))=λe2(N/M−1)Var_{\Omega^{(0)}}(\Psi_{(e)})=\lambda_e^2(N/M-1)VarΩ(0)​(Ψ(e)​)=λe2​(N/M−1) for the household. The second line separates the network-independent term of Corollary 1 from a correction for θ0≠θ1\theta_0\neq\theta_1θ0​=θ1​. When M=NM=NM=N energy is a universal input: the household is symmetrically exposed to energy through all goods, θ0\theta_0θ0​ drops out, and the term is λe(1−λe)(θ1−1)\lambda_e(1-\lambda_e)(\theta_1-1)λe​(1−λe​)(θ1​−1). As MMM falls, exposure becomes more heterogeneous, substitution in consumption matters more, and the amplification of negative energy shocks weakens; the sign can flip if MMM is low enough and θ0\theta_0θ0​ is far enough above one. A micro elasticity matters for the macro response only to the extent that the node it governs is unevenly exposed to the shock.

Proposition 8 (macro-influence). With a single factor, if all producers kkk have the same expenditure shares on iii and jjj, Ωki=Ωkj\Omega_{ki}=\Omega_{kj}Ωki​=Ωkj​, then the first-order impacts, the second-order impacts and all cross terms with any third producer lll are the same for iii and jjj. With the wage as numeraire, output equals real factor income and depends only on final goods prices, and a productivity shock lowers prices downstream without affecting prices upstream. Only the role of a producer as a supplier matters, not its role as a consumer of inputs.

Multiple Factors

Multiple factors allow for limited reallocation and decreasing returns through producer-specific or industry-specific fixed factors. Let Λf\Lambda_fΛf​ denote the Domar weight (income share) of factor fff and Λ\LambdaΛ the vector of factor shares.

d2log⁡Ydlog⁡Ae2=dΛedlog⁡Ae=(θ0−1)Λe(1−Λe)+(θ1−θ0)Λe(1−NMΛe)θ0+(θ1−θ0)1−NMΛe1−Λe(4.11.8.25)\frac{d^2\log Y}{d\log A_e^2}=\frac{d\Lambda_e}{d\log A_e}=\frac{(\theta_0-1)\Lambda_e(1-\Lambda_e)+(\theta_1-\theta_0)\Lambda_e\left(1-\frac{N}{M}\Lambda_e\right)}{\theta_0+(\theta_1-\theta_0)\frac{1-\frac{N}{M}\Lambda_e}{1-\Lambda_e}} \tag{4.11.8.25}dlogAe2​d2logY​=dlogAe​dΛe​​=θ0​+(θ1​−θ0​)1−Λe​1−MN​Λe​​(θ0​−1)Λe​(1−Λe​)+(θ1​−θ0​)Λe​(1−MN​Λe​)​(4.11.8.25)

Beyond CES

For a producer kkk with cost function Ck\mathbf{C}_kCk​, the Allen-Uzawa elasticity of substitution between inputs xxx and yyy is θk(x,y)=Ck (d2Ck/dpxdpy)/((dCk/dpx)(dCk/dpy))=ϵk(x,y)/Ωky\theta_k(x,y)=\mathbf{C}_k\,(d^2\mathbf{C}_k/dp_xdp_y)/((d\mathbf{C}_k/dp_x)(d\mathbf{C}_k/dp_y))=\epsilon_k(x,y)/\Omega_{ky}θk​(x,y)=Ck​(d2Ck​/dpx​dpy​)/((dCk​/dpx​)(dCk​/dpy​))=ϵk​(x,y)/Ωky​, where ϵk(x,y)\epsilon_k(x,y)ϵk​(x,y) is the elasticity of the demand of kkk for xxx with respect to the price of yyy. These elasticities are symmetric and satisfy the homogeneity identity ∑yΩkyθk(x,y)=0\sum_y\Omega_{ky}\theta_k(x,y)=0∑y​Ωky​θk​(x,y)=0. The input-output substitution operator is:

where δxy\delta_{xy}δxy​ is the Kronecker delta, Ψi(x)=Ψxi\Psi_i(x)=\Psi_{xi}Ψi​(x)=Ψxi​, and the expectation is over xxx and yyy drawn independently from the expenditure shares of kkk. In the CES case Φk(Ψ(i),Ψ(j))=(θk−1)CovΩ(k)(Ψ(i),Ψ(j))\Phi_k(\Psi_{(i)},\Psi_{(j)})=(\theta_k-1)Cov_{\Omega^{(k)}}(\Psi_{(i)},\Psi_{(j)})Φk​(Ψ(i)​,Ψ(j)​)=(θk​−1)CovΩ(k)​(Ψ(i)​,Ψ(j)​). All results generalize by this replacement; for example the Hessian of Proposition 9 becomes ∑kλkΦk(Ψ(i),Ψ(j))−∑f(dlog⁡Λf/dlog⁡Aj)∑kλkΦk(Ψ(i),Ψ(f))\sum_k\lambda_k\Phi_k(\Psi_{(i)},\Psi_{(j)})-\sum_f(d\log\Lambda_f/d\log A_j)\sum_k\lambda_k\Phi_k(\Psi_{(i)},\Psi_{(f)})∑k​λk​Φk​(Ψ(i)​,Ψ(j)​)−∑f​(dlogΛf​/dlogAj​)∑k​λk​Φk​(Ψ(i)​,Ψ(f)​). The operator measures how, when the price of jjj falls, kkk redirects expenditure toward iii. This characterizes the Hessian of the general economy, including non-homothetic technologies, since a non-homothetic function can be written as a constant-returns function with an additional fixed factor.

Quantitative Model and Calibration

The business-cycle application uses a nested-CES economy with industries i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,Ni=1,…,N:

YY‾=(∑i=1Nω0i(cic‾i)σ−1σ)σσ−1yiy‾i=Ai(ωil(lil‾i)θ−1θ+(1−ωil)(XiX‾i)θ−1θ)θθ−1XiX‾i=(∑j=1Nωij(xijx‾ij)ε−1ε)εε−1(4.11.8.27)\begin{aligned} \frac{Y}{\overline{Y}}&=\left(\sum_{i=1}^N\omega_{0i}\left(\frac{c_i}{\overline{c}_i}\right)^{\frac{\sigma-1}{\sigma}}\right)^{\frac{\sigma}{\sigma-1}}\\ \frac{y_i}{\overline{y}_i}&=A_i\left(\omega_{il}\left(\frac{l_i}{\overline{l}_i}\right)^{\frac{\theta-1}{\theta}}+(1-\omega_{il})\left(\frac{X_i}{\overline{X}_i}\right)^{\frac{\theta-1}{\theta}}\right)^{\frac{\theta}{\theta-1}}\\ \frac{X_i}{\overline{X}_i}&=\left(\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_{ij}\left(\frac{x_{ij}}{\overline{x}_{ij}}\right)^{\frac{\varepsilon-1}{\varepsilon}}\right)^{\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon-1}} \end{aligned} \tag{4.11.8.27}YY​y​i​yi​​Xi​Xi​​​=(i=1∑N​ω0i​(ci​ci​​)σσ−1​)σ−1σ​=Ai​(ωil​(li​li​​)θθ−1​+(1−ωil​)(Xi​Xi​​)θθ−1​)θ−1θ​=(j=1∑N​ωij​(xij​xij​​)εε−1​)ε−1ε​​(4.11.8.27)

where σ\sigmaσ is the elasticity of substitution in consumption, θ\thetaθ the elasticity between labor lil_ili​ and the intermediate bundle XiX_iXi​, and ε\varepsilonε the elasticity across intermediate inputs. Two labor markets are considered: no reallocation, where each industry has its own labor type, viewed as realistic for the short run, and full reallocation, where one factor is mobile across industries, viewed as suited to the medium and long run. Intermediate inputs are freely reallocated in both. The model is solved globally, not by approximation.

The data are the 88-sector US KLEMS annual input-output tables for 1960-2005, without government sectors, and the sectoral TFP series of Carvalho and Gabaix (2013). Expenditure shares match the 1982 input-output table. Sectoral shocks are independent and log-normal, log⁡Ai∼N(−Σii/2,Σii)\log A_i\sim\mathcal{N}(-\Sigma_{ii}/2,\Sigma_{ii})logAi​∼N(−Σii​/2,Σii​), where Σii\Sigma_{ii}Σii​ is the sample variance of log TFP growth of industry iii; the average correlation across sectors is below 5 percent. Shocks are calibrated at annual and at quadrennial horizons, and the quadrennial standard deviation is about twice the annual one. The benchmark is (σ,θ,ε)=(0.9,0.5,0.001)(\sigma,\theta,\varepsilon)=(0.9,0.5,0.001)(σ,θ,ε)=(0.9,0.5,0.001), based on Atalay (2017), Herrendorf, Rogerson and Valentinyi (2013), Oberfield and Raval (2014) and Boehm, Flaaen and Pandalai-Nayar (2017). The alternatives are (0.7,0.3,0.001)(0.7,0.3,0.001)(0.7,0.3,0.001), (0.9,0.6,0.2)(0.9,0.6,0.2)(0.9,0.6,0.2) and the nearly Cobb-Douglas (0.99,0.99,0.99)(0.99,0.99,0.99)(0.99,0.99,0.99). Because the volatility of Domar weights measures the size of second-order terms, it serves as a check: the target is σλ=∑iλ‾iσλi\sigma_\lambda=\sum_i\overline{\lambda}_i\sigma_{\lambda_i}σλ​=∑i​λi​σλi​​, where λ‾i\overline{\lambda}_iλi​ is here the time-series average Domar weight and σλi\sigma_{\lambda_i}σλi​​ the standard deviation of its log change. In the data σλ\sigma_\lambdaσλ​ is about 0.13 at annual and 0.27 at quadrennial frequency.

Quantitative Results

Moments of log output are computed from 50,000 draws. In the data the standard deviation of aggregate TFP growth is 0.015 annual and 0.030 quadrennial.

  • Domar weight volatility: with no reallocation the benchmark gives σλ\sigma_\lambdaσλ​ of 0.115 annual and 0.267 quadrennial, close to the data; the low-elasticity calibration overshoots (0.171 and 0.404) and the high-elasticity one undershoots (0.068 and 0.154). With full reallocation the benchmark gives 0.069 and 0.176, so that model is not nonlinear enough. The nearly Cobb-Douglas calibration gives at most 0.003.

  • Mean: in the benchmark without reallocation mean log output is −0.0034-0.0034−0.0034 annual and −0.0187-0.0187−0.0187 quadrennial, against −0.0011-0.0011−0.0011 and −0.0057-0.0057−0.0057 in the nearly Cobb-Douglas case, where the negative mean is the mechanical effect of log-normal shocks with unit mean in levels. The loss from nonlinearities is thus 0.23 percent annual and 1.30 percent quadrennial, compared with Lucas-style costs of about 0.01 and 0.05 percent. With full reallocation the paper reports losses of 0.1 and 0.46 percent (means of −0.0022-0.0022−0.0022 and −0.0113-0.0113−0.0113 against −0.0013-0.0013−0.0013 and −0.0058-0.0058−0.0058). The low-elasticity calibration without reallocation gives means of −0.0045-0.0045−0.0045 and −0.0270-0.0270−0.0270.

  • Standard deviation: about 0.011 to 0.012 annual in all calibrations, below the data, partly because shocks are assumed independent. At quadrennial frequency it is 0.030 in the benchmark without reallocation and 0.025 under Cobb-Douglas.

  • Skewness and excess kurtosis: in the benchmark without reallocation skewness is −0.18-0.18−0.18 annual and −1.11-1.11−1.11 quadrennial and excess kurtosis is 0.1 and 3.6; the low-elasticity calibration gives −2.18-2.18−2.18 and 12.7 at quadrennial frequency. With full reallocation the benchmark gives skewness of −0.08-0.08−0.08 and −0.28-0.28−0.28. The Cobb-Douglas economy has essentially zero skewness and excess kurtosis. Rare disasters thus arise endogenously, without fat-tailed shocks or fat-tailed Domar weights.

  • Industry shocks: “oil and gas” and “retail trade (excluding automobiles)” have similar sales shares. Output is roughly log-linear in shocks to retail trade and strongly concave in shocks to oil and gas, which produces the largest output loss of all industries after a large negative shock. Oil and gas is close to a universal input, so the low upstream elasticity θ\thetaθ matters more than σ\sigmaσ, and it uses few intermediate inputs, so resources cannot be moved in to raise its output. This matches the finding of Hamilton (2003) that oil price increases matter much more than decreases.

Oil Shocks and Baumol's Cost Disease

The second exercise is nonparametric and uses observed changes in Domar weights instead of a structural model.

Proposition 10. Up to the second order in the vector of shocks Δ\DeltaΔ:

log⁡(Y(A+Δ)/Y(A))=12[λ(A+Δ)+λ(A)]′(log⁡(A+Δ)−log⁡(A))(4.11.8.28)\log\left(Y(A+\Delta)/Y(A)\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left[\lambda(A+\Delta)+\lambda(A)\right]'\left(\log(A+\Delta)-\log(A)\right) \tag{4.11.8.28}log(Y(A+Δ)/Y(A))=21​[λ(A+Δ)+λ(A)]′(log(A+Δ)−log(A))(4.11.8.28)

The proof combines a lemma of Theil (1967), which approximates the change in a function by the average of its gradients at the two endpoints with a third-order error, with Hulten's theorem, which identifies the gradient of log⁡Y\log YlogY with the vector of Domar weights λ(A)\lambda(A)λ(A). Averaging weights over two periods is the idea of Tornqvist (1936). The formula is a first-order approximation of the Domar weight inside the exact integral of λ dlog⁡A\lambda\,d\log AλdlogA. It is useful only ex post, since ex ante one needs the structural results to predict the change in Domar weights. Global expenditure on crude oil rose from 1.8 percent of world GDP in 1972 to 7.6 percent in 1979 and was back at its earlier level by 1986. The price of crude rose from 3.5 dollars per barrel in 1972 to 11 dollars in 1974 and peaked at 37 dollars in 1980. Treating oil as an endowment, the shock is the cumulative change in demeaned log growth of world crude production from 1973 to 1980, which is −13-13−13 percent. The first-order impact is 1.8 percent times −13-13−13 percent, or −0.23-0.23−0.23 percent of world output. The second-order impact uses the average weight of 4.7 percent and equals −0.61-0.61−0.61 percent. The amplification factor of about 2.6 does not depend on the size of the shock, and it arises without financial or demand-side frictions, endogenous labor supply or capital accumulation.

The third exercise uses World KLEMS data for the United States from 1948 to 2014. Aggregate TFP growth is measured with Domar weights updated every period, with weights fixed at their 1948 values, and with the average of initial and final weights:

Δlog⁡TFPnonlinear=∑i=1N∑t=19482013λi,t(log⁡Ai,t+1−log⁡Ai,t)Δlog⁡TFP1st order=∑i=1Nλi,1948(log⁡Ai,2014−log⁡Ai,1948)Δlog⁡TFP2nd order=12∑i=1N(λi,1948+λi,2014)(log⁡Ai,2014−log⁡Ai,1948)(4.11.8.29)\begin{aligned} \Delta\log TFP^{\text{nonlinear}}&=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=1948}^{2013}\lambda_{i,t}\left(\log A_{i,t+1}-\log A_{i,t}\right)\\ \Delta\log TFP^{\text{1st order}}&=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_{i,1948}\left(\log A_{i,2014}-\log A_{i,1948}\right)\\ \Delta\log TFP^{\text{2nd order}}&=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N\left(\lambda_{i,1948}+\lambda_{i,2014}\right)\left(\log A_{i,2014}-\log A_{i,1948}\right) \end{aligned} \tag{4.11.8.29}ΔlogTFPnonlinearΔlogTFP1st orderΔlogTFP2nd order​=i=1∑N​t=1948∑2013​λi,t​(logAi,t+1​−logAi,t​)=i=1∑N​λi,1948​(logAi,2014​−logAi,1948​)=21​i=1∑N​(λi,1948​+λi,2014​)(logAi,2014​−logAi,1948​)​(4.11.8.29)

The first line is a left Riemann sum for the exact integral, and the second is the growth that a log-linear (Cobb-Douglas) economy would have had with the same path of industry TFP. Counterfactual growth is around 87 percent and actual growth 68 percent, so nonlinearities reduced aggregate TFP growth by around 19 percentage points; the second-order measure is much closer to the nonlinear one. This is Baumol's cost disease: the sales shares of industries with low productivity growth rise over time. The calculation covers both complementarities and non-homotheticities, since both change Domar weights. The paper notes that in inefficient economies the terms characterized here can become first order.

This equation defines real aggregate output. A representative final-demand agent chooses consumption cic_ici​ of each of the NNN goods to maximize the aggregator D\mathcal{D}D, taking prices pip_ipi​ as given. The right-hand side of the budget constraint is total income: payments wflfw_fl_fwf​lf​ to the FFF factors in fixed supply plus profits πi\pi_iπi​. Both sides equal nominal GDP, so the constraint says that final expenditure equals value added.

The aggregator D\mathcal{D}D has constant returns to scale. This buys two things. First, YYY is a well-defined quantity index: there is an ideal price index PPP with PY=∑ipiciPY=\sum_ip_ic_iPY=∑i​pi​ci​, so that YYY is nominal GDP deflated by PPP. Second, the first-order conditions of the problem are

∂D∂ci=κpi,Y=∑i∂D∂cici=κ∑ipici,\frac{\partial\mathcal{D}}{\partial c_i}=\kappa p_i,\qquad Y=\sum_i\frac{\partial\mathcal{D}}{\partial c_i}c_i=\kappa\sum_ip_ic_i,∂ci​∂D​=κpi​,Y=i∑​∂ci​∂D​ci​=κi∑​pi​ci​,

where κ\kappaκ is the multiplier on the budget constraint and the second relation is Euler's theorem. Hence κ=1/P\kappa=1/Pκ=1/P, which is the step that turns shadow values into prices in the proof of equation (3). Homotheticity rules out income effects in final demand; the note explains that non-homothetic cases can still be handled by adding fixed factors. Because the economy is efficient, YYY is also the value of a planning problem, and it becomes a function Y(A1,…,AN)Y(A_1,\dots,A_N)Y(A1​,…,AN​) of the productivities introduced in equation (2).

The first line gives the technology and profit of producer iii. Output yiy_iyi​ is produced from factors lifl_{if}lif​ and intermediate inputs xijx_{ij}xij​ (the amount of good jjj used by iii), scaled by a Hicks-neutral productivity AiA_iAi​. Profit πi\pi_iπi​ is revenue minus factor and intermediate costs. The second line states market clearing: output of good iii is used as an intermediate by all producers jjj or consumed, and the fixed supply lfl_flf​ of each factor is allocated across producers.

Since FiF_iFi​ has constant returns and firms are competitive, πi=0\pi_i=0πi​=0 in equilibrium and price equals marginal cost. The economy has no distortions, so the first welfare theorem applies and the equilibrium solves

Y(A1,…,AN)=max⁡ D(c1,…,cN)s.t.ci+∑jxji≤AiFi(⋅),∑ilif≤lf.Y(A_1,\dots,A_N)=\max\ \mathcal{D}(c_1,\dots,c_N)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad c_i+\sum_jx_{ji}\leq A_iF_i(\cdot),\quad\sum_il_{if}\leq l_f .Y(A1​,…,AN​)=max D(c1​,…,cN​)s.t.ci​+j∑​xji​≤Ai​Fi​(⋅),i∑​lif​≤lf​.

This planning representation is what makes the envelope argument behind equation (3) work. The structure is more general than it looks: decreasing returns are a fixed factor specific to iii, limited reallocation is a factor specific to a subset of producers, and an input-specific shock is a Hicks-neutral shock to a fictitious producer that relabels the input. A shock to the supply of factor fff is treated the same way, with AfA_fAf​ scaling lfl_flf​. All derivatives in the note are taken at the steady state where every Ai=1A_i=1Ai​=1.

The input-output multiplier ξ\xiξ is defined as the response of log output to a uniform one percent increase in all productivities. The second equality is immediate from equation (3): each term of the sum is a Domar weight, so ξ\xiξ is total sales divided by GDP.

Without intermediate inputs all sales are final sales and ξ=1\xi=1ξ=1. With intermediate inputs gross output exceeds value added and ξ>1\xi>1ξ>1: a good that is used to produce other goods is counted every time it is sold. In the roundabout economy of equation (14) with labor share ω1l\omega_{1l}ω1l​,

ξ=1+(1−ω1l)+(1−ω1l)2+⋯=1ω1l,\xi=1+(1-\omega_{1l})+(1-\omega_{1l})^2+\dots=\frac{1}{\omega_{1l}} ,ξ=1+(1−ω1l​)+(1−ω1l​)2+⋯=ω1l​1​,

so a labor share of one half gives ξ=2\xi=2ξ=2. In this sense ξ\xiξ measures aggregate returns to scale in the reproducible inputs.

The multiplier is not a structural constant. Its elasticity dlog⁡ξ/dlog⁡Aid\log\xi/d\log A_idlogξ/dlogAi​ records whether a shock moves spending toward reproducible goods (sales) or toward primary factors (whose income is GDP). These are the primitives of the horizontal economy. Each good iii is produced by a Cobb-Douglas function of a specific labor lisil_{is_i}lisi​​, which only producer iii can use, and a general labor ligl_{ig}lig​, which can move across producers; ωg\omega_gωg​ is the output elasticity of general labor. There are no intermediate inputs, so consumption equals output and ξ=1\xi=1ξ=1. Final demand is CES with elasticity θ0\theta_0θ0​ and weights ω0i\omega_{0i}ω0i​ that sum to one.

All variables are divided by their steady-state values (overlines). This is the technology of the roundabout economy: a single good y1y_1y1​ is produced from labor l1l_1l1​ and from its own output x1x_1x1​ with a CES function of elasticity θ1\theta_1θ1​. This is the production function of a node in the standard-form representation. Every CES nest of the original economy is relabeled as a separate node iii with a single elasticity θi\theta_iθi​; a producer with several nests becomes several nodes linked by intermediate flows. Node 000 is the household, whose output y0y_0y0​ is real GDP and whose productivity is fixed; nodes 111 to NNN are goods; inputs jjj run over the NNN goods and the FFF factors, which are endowments. The weights ωij\omega_{ij}ωij​ sum to one, and because quantities are normalized by steady-state values they equal steady-state cost shares, ωij=Ωij\omega_{ij}=\Omega_{ij}ωij​=Ωij​ of equation (17).

pi=1Ai(∑jωijpj1−θi)11−θi,Ωij=ωijAiθi−1(pjpi)1−θi.p_i=\frac{1}{A_i}\left(\sum_j\omega_{ij}p_j^{1-\theta_i}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\theta_i}},\qquad\Omega_{ij}=\omega_{ij}A_i^{\theta_i-1}\left(\frac{p_j}{p_i}\right)^{1-\theta_i}.pi​=Ai​1​(j∑​ωij​pj1−θi​​)1−θi​1​,Ωij​=ωij​Aiθi​−1​(pi​pj​​)1−θi​.

This single property drives equations (18) to (25). The form rules out non-CES substitution patterns within a node, which equation (26) later relaxes, but it is otherwise general: arbitrary nests, arbitrary network, any number of factors.

The first line defines the steady-state input-output matrix and its Leontief inverse. Ωij\Omega_{ij}Ωij​ is the share of the cost (equal to revenue) of node iii spent on input jjj; rows are buyers and columns are suppliers. The matrix covers all N+1+FN+1+FN+1+F nodes; the household row holds final expenditure shares and factor rows are zero. Expanding the inverse,

The household row gives the Domar weights, Ψ0i=λi\Psi_{0i}=\lambda_iΨ0i​=λi​ and Ψ0f=Λf\Psi_{0f}=\Lambda_fΨ0f​=Λf​, and for every node the exposures to the factors sum to one, ∑fΨlf=1\sum_f\Psi_{lf}=1∑f​Ψlf​=1.

It is zero if all inputs of kkk are equally exposed to iii (or to jjj), in particular if kkk has a single input. This is the quantitative model, a three-level nested-CES economy. Line one: the household aggregates consumption of the NNN industries with elasticity σ\sigmaσ and weights ω0i\omega_{0i}ω0i​. Line two: industry iii combines labor lil_ili​ and an intermediate bundle XiX_iXi​ with elasticity θ\thetaθ; ωil\omega_{il}ωil​ is its steady-state labor share and AiA_iAi​ its Hicks-neutral productivity. Line three: the bundle aggregates intermediate goods xijx_{ij}xij​ with elasticity ε\varepsilonε and weights ωij\omega_{ij}ωij​. All quantities are relative to steady state, so the weights are read directly from input-output tables (the 1982 table), and the three elasticities are the only free technology parameters. Here σ\sigmaσ is an elasticity, not the standard deviation of equation (9).

In the standard form of equation (16) each industry is two nodes, one for the value-added and intermediate nest (θ\thetaθ) and one for the bundle (ε\varepsilonε), so equations (18) and (22) apply with θk∈{σ,θ,ε}\theta_k\in\{\sigma,\theta,\varepsilon\}θk​∈{σ,θ,ε}. The labor market closes the model in one of two ways: one mobile factor, where equation (18) applies, or one specific factor per industry, where equations (22) and (23) apply. The benchmark (σ,θ,ε)=(0.9,0.5,0.001)(\sigma,\theta,\varepsilon)=(0.9,0.5,0.001)(σ,θ,ε)=(0.9,0.5,0.001) makes intermediates nearly Leontief; by equation (18) how much each elasticity matters depends on how unevenly the corresponding nodes are exposed to the shocked industry. The model is solved globally, so its moments include all higher-order terms; the second-order formulas serve to interpret them.

Let a=log⁡Aa=\log Aa=logA and g(a)=log⁡Yg(a)=\log Yg(a)=logY, and let d=log⁡(A+Δ)−log⁡Ad=\log(A+\Delta)-\log Ad=log(A+Δ)−logA be the vector of log changes. Expand ggg to second order and its gradient to first order around aaa, with Hessian HHH:

g(a+d)−g(a)=∇g(a)′d+12d′Hd+O(∥d∥3),∇g(a+d)=∇g(a)+Hd+O(∥d∥2).g(a+d)-g(a)=\nabla g(a)'d+\tfrac12d'Hd+O(\|d\|^3),\qquad\nabla g(a+d)=\nabla g(a)+Hd+O(\|d\|^2).g(a+d)−g(a)=∇g(a)′d+21​d′Hd+O(∥d∥3),∇g(a+d)=∇g(a)+Hd+O(∥d∥2).

Use the second expansion to eliminate the Hessian: Hd=∇g(a+d)−∇g(a)Hd=\nabla g(a+d)-\nabla g(a)Hd=∇g(a+d)−∇g(a) up to second order, so

g(a+d)−g(a)=∇g(a)′d+12(∇g(a+d)−∇g(a))′d+O(∥d∥3)=12(∇g(a+d)+∇g(a))′d+O(∥d∥3).g(a+d)-g(a)=\nabla g(a)'d+\tfrac12\left(\nabla g(a+d)-\nabla g(a)\right)'d+O(\|d\|^3)=\tfrac12\left(\nabla g(a+d)+\nabla g(a)\right)'d+O(\|d\|^3).g(a+d)−g(a)=∇g(a)′d+21​(∇g(a+d)−∇g(a))′d+O(∥d∥3)=21​(∇g(a+d)+∇g(a))′d+O(∥d∥3).

This is Theil's lemma: the average of the gradients at the two endpoints captures the second-order term without knowledge of HHH. By equation (3), which holds at every point of an efficient economy, ∇g(a)=λ(A)\nabla g(a)=\lambda(A)∇g(a)=λ(A) and ∇g(a+d)=λ(A+Δ)\nabla g(a+d)=\lambda(A+\Delta)∇g(a+d)=λ(A+Δ). Hence

log⁡(Y(A+Δ)/Y(A))≈12(λ(A+Δ)+λ(A))′(log⁡(A+Δ)−log⁡(A)),\log\left(Y(A+\Delta)/Y(A)\right)\approx\tfrac12\left(\lambda(A+\Delta)+\lambda(A)\right)'\left(\log(A+\Delta)-\log(A)\right),log(Y(A+Δ)/Y(A))≈21​(λ(A+Δ)+λ(A))′(log(A+Δ)−log(A)),

with an error of third order; the equality sign in the note is to be read in this sense. It is the trapezoid rule for the exact line integral of λ′dlog⁡A\lambda'd\log Aλ′dlogA. In the oil application the shock is −0.13-0.13−0.13 and the weights are 0.0180.0180.018 before and 0.0760.0760.076 after: the first-order effect is 0.018×(−0.13)≈−0.00230.018\times(-0.13)\approx-0.00230.018×(−0.13)≈−0.0023, and the second-order effect is 12(0.018+0.076)×(−0.13)=0.047×(−0.13)≈−0.0061\tfrac12(0.018+0.076)\times(-0.13)=0.047\times(-0.13)\approx-0.006121​(0.018+0.076)×(−0.13)=0.047×(−0.13)≈−0.0061. The ratio is 0.047/0.018≈2.60.047/0.018\approx2.60.047/0.018≈2.6 whatever the size of the shock.

The three lines are measures of cumulative aggregate TFP growth in the United States between 1948 and 2014, built from industry TFP Ai,tA_{i,t}Ai,t​ and Domar weights λi,t\lambda_{i,t}λi,t​. They differ only in the weights.

The nonlinear measure chains annual changes with the weights of each year. By equation (3) the exact change in log output is the line integral of ∑iλi dlog⁡Ai\sum_i\lambda_i\,d\log A_i∑i​λi​dlogAi​ along the path of productivities, and the first line is a left Riemann sum for it; with annual steps the weights barely move within a step, so this is treated as the truth. The first-order measure freezes the weights in 1948. It is what Hulten's approximation predicts from the initial year, and it is exact if the economy is Cobb-Douglas, in which case Domar weights never change. The second-order measure is equation (28) applied once to the whole period, with the average of the 1948 and 2014 weights.

The gap between the first two lines is a covariance between weight changes and productivity growth:

Δlog⁡TFPnonlinear−Δlog⁡TFP1st order=∑i=1N∑t=19482013(λi,t−λi,1948)(log⁡Ai,t+1−log⁡Ai,t).\Delta\log TFP^{\text{nonlinear}}-\Delta\log TFP^{\text{1st order}}=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=1948}^{2013}\left(\lambda_{i,t}-\lambda_{i,1948}\right)\left(\log A_{i,t+1}-\log A_{i,t}\right).ΔlogTFPnonlinear−ΔlogTFP1st order=i=1∑N​t=1948∑2013​(λi,t​−λi,1948​)(logAi,t+1​−logAi,t​).

It is negative when industries with slow productivity growth gain sales share over time, which complementarity implies by equation (4). The note reports about 68 against 87 percent, a gap of about 19 points (Baumol's cost disease). The calculation uses only data and efficiency; no elasticities are estimated.
